title: The Anatomy of a Complete MCP Exchange

questions.question: A single MCP tool call can exercise every domain in the MCPA blueprint at once. Which statement best captures how that happens?
options: Each domain corresponds to a different transport, so no single exchange crosses more than one
One call carries a negotiated version, a validated schema, a consent decision, and an audit entry together
The five domains run as separate protocols, so a single call can only ever touch one of them
Only the Security and Governance domain applies once a server connection has already been approved
questions.explanation: A production tool call is one continuous exchange, and the version negotiated at the handshake, the schema a server enforces, the consent a host requires, and the entry an audit log records all describe properties of that same exchange, not separate protocols.

questions.question: In the capstone demo, a client sends tools/call for restart_service with no arguments, even though the tool's schema requires one. What does the server return?
options: A JSON-RPC error with code -32601, reporting an unknown method
A successful result that silently substitutes a default value for the missing argument
A JSON-RPC error with code -32602, reporting the missing required argument
A JSON-RPC error with code -32600, reporting a malformed request envelope
questions.explanation: Missing a required argument is an invalid params condition, and JSON-RPC 2.0 reserves -32602 for exactly that case, distinct from an unknown method or a malformed envelope, and a conformant server must reject the call rather than guessing a value to substitute.

questions.question: The capstone demo marks restart_service with a destructiveHint annotation. What role does that annotation play in the exchange?
options: It replaces the input schema, so the server no longer validates arguments for that tool
It sets the JSON-RPC error code the server must return if the call fails
It tells the server which programming language the tool handler is written in
It lets the host decide, before sending the call, whether to require the user's consent
questions.explanation: Tool annotations such as destructiveHint travel with the discovered tool list, so a host can read them and decide whether a side-effecting call needs explicit user approval before the request is even sent, independent of the schema the server later validates.

questions.question: After a run, host.audit_log.verify() recomputes every entry's hash from its own fields and the previous entry's hash. What does a passing result actually demonstrate?
options: That the recorded entries form a chain and none were altered after being written
That the server validated every argument against its schema before executing any handler
That every tool call in the run returned a successful result rather than an error
That the user granted consent for every side-effecting tool called during the run
questions.explanation: A hash chain links each entry to the one before it, so recomputing every hash and comparing it to the stored value only succeeds if the sequence is complete and no entry was inserted, removed, or edited after it was appended to the log.

questions.question: A side-effecting call is attempted before the user has granted consent. Where in the exchange does the refusal happen?
options: At the transport layer, which drops the connection without sending a response
At the host, before any request for that call reaches the server
At the model, which silently ignores the tool the host had offered it
At the server, after it has already executed the tool's handler
questions.explanation: Consent is a host-side policy decision informed by the tool's advertised annotations, so a missing approval is caught before the client ever transmits the call, which is why the refusal carries no request id: nothing was sent to the server to respond to.

questions.question: Once a tool call succeeds, its result crosses back from the server into the host. Why does the capstone treat that moment as security relevant, not just a data return?
options: Because the audit log discards its entries as soon as a result is returned
Because JSON-RPC forbids a server from returning anything beyond a single string value
Because the server is a separate program, and its output becomes untrusted input to the model
Because the result is always larger in size than the request that produced it
questions.explanation: The server sits outside the host's own trust boundary, so whatever it returns is external content entering the model's context; schema validation and consent govern the outgoing call, but the returning result still needs the same scrutiny as any other untrusted input.
